outcome: Nothing has settled, bounded or moved the question since 26 January 2024: on every source read, as of 12 October 2026, whether the nim-sequence of Grundy's game is eventually periodic is still open. The only in-window items touching the game are a 2025 OEIS comment on the rules, 2025 OEIS tables extending the computed values to n = 200000 (files not opened), an 11 October 2026 refresh of Flammenkamp's octal-games page whose Grundy's Game row matches his 2021 data, and neighbouring papers on other games that do not mention Grundy's game.
problem_asks: Whether the nim-sequence of Grundy's game is eventually periodic. Written from the statement alone: the sequence is G(n), the Sprague–Grundy value of a heap of n tokens, for n = 0, 1, 2, …; the question is whether there exist N and p ≥ 1 such that G(n + p) = G(n) for all n ≥ N. That is the only part the statement asks. It asks for no bound on N or on p, and it does not ask for the period to be computed. Grundy's game is the heap-splitting game in which a move divides one heap into two non-empty heaps of unequal size; heaps of size 1 or 2 cannot be split.

events.what_happened: Elwyn Berlekamp, John Horton Conway and Richard Guy conjectured, in Winning Ways for your Mathematical Plays (Academic Press, 1982), that the nim-sequence of Grundy's game eventually becomes periodic. Wikipedia's article cites this book as the source of the conjecture. I did not open the book; the attribution comes from the Wikipedia article, which I did open.
events.delivers: States the conjecture only: that the sequence is eventually periodic. It gives the first few values, no period and no proof.
events.remains: All of problem_asks. A conjecture is not a result, so nothing in problem_asks is answered.
events.time_since_posted: About 44 years as of October 2026. No argument was offered, so there was nothing to check.
events.direction: Asserts the answer yes to the question: the sequence is eventually periodic.

events.what_happened: The OEIS entry A002188 carries a formula note, added by N. J. Sloane on 3 January 2016, that attributes to Guy (Fair Game, 1989, p. 96) the statement: “Mike Guy has computed ten million values, but a discernible pattern remains elusive.” I did not open Fair Game. The OEIS text says “Mike Guy”; the book is by Richard K. Guy. Search summaries could not settle whether these are the same person, so the attribution is unverified.
events.delivers: Reports, as a claim in an OEIS note, that about 10⁷ nim-values were computed with no pattern found. This is a finite computation and establishes nothing about periodicity.
events.doubts: Single secondary attribution, from an OEIS note; the book text was not read. The figure is a lower bound on earlier computing and is consistent with Dan Hoey's later run to 11×10⁹ (event hoey-1995-1996-11e9). It is not independent evidence about the computing history.
events.direction: Consistent with the conjecture as far as it goes; no bearing on the universal claim.
people: Richard K. Guy (per the OEIS attribution “Mike Guy”; identity not resolved)

events.what_happened: Guy and Nowakowski's unsolved-problems list for combinatorial games (begun by Guy in 1991 and updated in the Games of No Chance series) has a 2009 column stating that Grundy's game has been analysed, first by Dan Hoey and later by Achim Flammenkamp, “as far as heaps of 235 beans”. The 2002 version asks whether all finite octal games are ultimately periodic and lists Grundy's Game among the outstanding particular cases. I did not open these documents. Both statements come from search snippets. The PDFs returned binary content when fetched. This column is the likely origin of the figure “235” in Wikipedia; that link is my inference.
events.revisions: 2002 list; 2009 column; 2015 and 2017 editions with new section-letter numbering; 2025 edition (Games of No Chance vol. 71), per search snippets.
events.delivers: A status statement: the game had been computed to heap size 235 at the date of the column. It establishes no periodicity.
events.doubts: Known only from search snippets; the column text was not read. The 2002 and 2009 wording may differ, and the 2025 edition's entry for Grundy's game could not be read at all.
events.direction: No direction on the universal claim; a status report on computing only.

events.what_happened: Dan Hoey computed G(n) for all n up to 11×10⁹ between August 1995 and March 1996. Achim Flammenkamp's page “Sprague-Grundy Values of Grundy's Game” (grundy.html) reports this: “From August 1995 until March 1996 Dan Hoey computed all values G(n) up to 11*10^9.” The date is the completion of the run. The page does not date the public posting.
events.revisions: grundy.html last updated 2021-04-10 (per the fetched page).
events.delivers: Finite verification: the nim-values G(n) for all n ≤ 11×10⁹. This is finitely many instances of a universal claim and establishes no period.
events.directly_checkable: The recurrence can be checked by hand for small n. G(n) is the mex of G(a) XOR G(n−a) over all a with 1 ≤ a < n and a ≠ n−a, with G(0) = G(1) = G(2) = 0. I checked n = 3 to 8 against the OEIS terms 1, 0, 2, 1, 0, 2 and they agree.
events.doubts: Single-author computation, reported by the author who later published the table. No independent recomputation, code or log was found in the sources read.
events.direction: Finite check; consistent with, but does not decide, the conjecture.

events.what_happened: Flammenkamp's grundy.html records an earlier milestone, “n ≤ 5·2³² (December 2000)”, for the computed values of the game. The sentence comes from one summarising fetch of the page; a second fetch of the same page did not repeat it. The 2000 run was superseded by the 2012 run (event flammenkamp-2012-run-G-284944236543).
events.revisions: grundy.html last updated 2021-04-10 (per the fetched page).
events.delivers: Finite computation of nim-values up to n ≤ 5·2³². It establishes no period.
events.doubts: Read from a single summarising fetch of the page. No independent check was found.
events.direction: Finite check; no direction on the universal claim.

events.what_happened: Flammenkamp's grundy.html says: “Starting on November 1st 2012, I made two runs finally reached G(284944236543) on 2012-11-25 and abort the job.” The same page says: “In autum 2012 I tracked more octal-games and Grundy's Game to higher positions.” It also says: “To discover a possible periodicity in its sg-values, I protocoled all n with G(n) >= 286”, and that if the sparse large values die out “the infinte sequence of the G(n) must become periodic”. The page's frequency table covers heap sizes 0–238 and lists 1287 sparse values, the last at n = 48,399,022. The page is last updated 10 April 2021. This quotation was confirmed in two separate fetches of the page.
events.revisions: grundy.html last updated 2021-04-10; octal.html last updated 2026-10-11 (event flammenkamp-octal-page-2026-10-11).
events.delivers: A run that reached index n = 284,944,236,543 (about 2.8×10¹¹) and was then aborted. The published frequency table covers heap sizes 0–238. The sparse values listed run to n = 48,399,022. The page does not say what was verified between those points. Finite computation; no period is established.
events.directly_checkable: The recurrence in event hoey-1995-1996-11e9 can reproduce small values. The value at 284,944,236,543 itself is not reported on the page.
events.doubts: The page does not say how the value at 2.8×10¹¹ was obtained or verified. The run was aborted, and no code or independent check is cited. The page's remark that the sequence must be periodic if the sparse values die out is a conditional, not a result; the page does not show that they die out. The page's own log of G(n) ≥ 286 is described only as showing no pattern found.
events.direction: Finite computation; no direction on the universal claim.

events.what_happened: “Partition games” (Antoine Dailly, Eric Duchêne, Urban Larsson, Gabrielle Paris), arXiv:1803.02621, submitted 7 March 2018 (v2 24 October 2019; v3 15 May 2020). It studies CUT, two-player partition games in which a move splits one heap into c+1 non-empty heaps for some c in a ruleset C, with no constraint on part sizes. It proves periodic or arithmetic-periodic Sprague–Grundy sequences for several rulesets and gives a computational testing condition. Section 4.1 says that Grundy's game needs unequal parts, which CUT does not impose, and concludes “Hence, grundy's game is not in octal.” So Grundy's game lies outside this paper's class. The introduction says ruleset C = {1,2} “remains a mystery”. These quotations come from a partial read of the ar5iv full text (the first 100,000 of 111,721 characters).
events.revisions: v1 7 Mar 2018; v2 24 Oct 2019; v3 15 May 2020 (current, per the arXiv abstract page).
events.delivers: Periodicity for other CUT rulesets. The paper says Grundy's game is outside its class, so it gives no result on Grundy's game. The C = {1,2} case it calls open is a different game.
events.remains: All of problem_asks, since the paper does not address Grundy's game.
events.time_since_posted: About 8.6 years as of October 2026. No journal publication was established in the sources read.
events.direction: No direction on Grundy's game. This is a neighbouring class that the paper itself excludes Grundy's game from.

events.what_happened: Allan C. Wechsler's comment on OEIS A002188, dated 22 March 2025 on the fetched page, describes the rules. A move divides a heap into two unequal parts, and heaps of 1 or 2 cannot be split. It notes that Grundy's game is not an octal game, because that formalism cannot express the unequal-split rule. The comment makes no claim about periodicity. Recorded as discounted: it is a rules clarification, not progress.
events.delivers: A rules clarification only. It establishes nothing about the nim-sequence.
events.direction: No direction on the universal claim.

events.what_happened: The OEIS entry A002188 links two tables attributed to David Cleaver: a b-file for n = 0–20000 (first 10,000 terms from Eric M. Schmidt), at https://oeis.org/A002188/b002188.txt, and a(n) for n = 0–200000, at https://oeis.org/A002188/a002188.txt. A Python program is attributed to David Cleaver, Mar 22 2025. I did not open the table files, so their contents and posting date are unverified. The year 2025 comes from the code attribution on the OEIS page.
events.delivers: If the file matches its description, a finite list of nim-values to n = 200,000. These are finitely many instances, and they establish no period.
events.directly_checkable: The values can be recomputed from the recurrence described in event hoey-1995-1996-11e9.
events.doubts: Table contents not verified, since the files were not opened. The 2025 date is only the code attribution.
events.direction: Finite computation; no direction on the universal claim.
people: Eric M. Schmidt (first 10,000 terms of the b-file)

events.what_happened: “Additive sink subtraction” (Anjali Bhagat, Urban Larsson, Hikaru Manabe, Takahiro Yamashita), arXiv:2601.18715, submitted 26 January 2026 (v3 16 March 2026). Its abstract, read on the arXiv abstract page, concerns subtraction games. It states that every subtraction game with a finite move set has an eventually periodic nim-sequence, and it claims a complete solution for the additive case. It does not concern heap-splitting games, and the abstract does not mention Grundy's game.
events.revisions: v1 26 Jan 2026; v3 16 Mar 2026 (v2 not recorded).
events.delivers: Eventual periodicity for subtraction games with finite move sets, and a formula for the additive case. It says nothing about Grundy's game, which is not a subtraction game.
events.direction: No direction on Grundy's game. Neighbouring game class.

events.what_happened: “Additive Subtraction Games” (Urban Larsson, Hikaru Manabe), arXiv:2603.10414, submitted 11 March 2026 (v2 29 March 2026). Its abstract, read on the arXiv abstract page, determines the nim-value structure of additive subtraction games in the primitive quadratic regime and gives a closed formula for the P-positions. Grundy's game and octal games are not mentioned on the abstract page.
events.delivers: A closed formula for P-positions in one family of subtraction games. It says nothing about Grundy's game.
events.direction: No direction on Grundy's game. Neighbouring game class.

events.what_happened: “A Finite Automaton Approach to Combinatorial Games” (Kai Liang), arXiv:2608.13273, submitted 13 August 2026 (v2 29 August 2026). Its abstract, read on the arXiv abstract page, solves most two-digit partizan octal games, proposes a partizan version of Guy's conjecture on octal games, and proves that outcomes and Sprague–Grundy values of Kotzig's nim are periodic under normal and misère play. Grundy's game and heap-splitting games are not mentioned on the abstract page. The full text was not read.
events.delivers: Results on partizan octal games and Kotzig's nim. It states nothing about Grundy's game. Guy's conjecture is named as the context, and Grundy's game is among the outstanding cases of the Guy–Nowakowski list, but this paper's partizan analogue is not shown to bear on Grundy's game.
events.remains: All of problem_asks. Whether the partizan analogue bears on Grundy's game is not established.
events.doubts: Abstract page only; the full text was not read, so any mention of Grundy's game or of AI use in the body or acknowledgements is unchecked.
events.direction: No direction on Grundy's game. Relevant only to the broader octal-game conjecture, which Grundy's game is listed under.

events.what_happened: Flammenkamp's octal-games page (wwwhomes.uni-bielefeld.de/achim/octal.html) carries the footer “last updated 2026-10-11 22:50 UTC+2”. Its table row for Grundy's Game gives max n 239, 1287 sparse values, last rare index 48399022, maximum G-value 297 and 42 lost values. It lists the game among the unsettled cases and gives no period. The same sparse data (1287 values, last at 48399022, heap range 0–238) appears on the separate Grundy page last updated 10 April 2021 (event flammenkamp-2012-run-G-284944236543). I found no sign of an extension beyond the 2021 data.
events.delivers: A re-presentation of the 2021 data, with no extension of the contiguous range and no period. Finite instances only.
events.time_since_posted: Updated the day before this record was made.
events.doubts: The comparison with the 2021 page rests on two summarising fetches that report identical headline numbers (1287 sparse values, last at 48,399,022, heap range 0–238). I did not compare the full tables, so a change inside the table cannot be excluded from what I read.

summary: Nothing has settled, bounded or moved the question since 26 January 2024. Every source I could read still treats eventual periodicity of the nim-sequence of Grundy's game as open. Wikipedia's article, last edited 15 March 2026, says the question is unresolved and gives 235 computed values, citing Winning Ways (1982) and Flammenkamp. Two Flammenkamp pages are the main computational sources. His grundy.html (last updated 10 April 2021) tabulates heap sizes 0–238, reports a 2012 run that reached G(284944236543) on 25 November 2012 (aborted), and builds on Dan Hoey's 1995–96 computation to 11×10⁹ and a December 2000 milestone of 5·2³². The figure 235 is therefore stale; it traces to a 2009 Guy–Nowakowski column, known to me only from a search snippet. The octal page (updated 11 October 2026) shows the same Grundy row as the 2021 data, so the refresh adds no visible extension. The OEIS entry A002188 adds three in-window items: a rules-only comment by Allan Wechsler (22 March 2025), David Cleaver's tables to n = 200000 (files not opened), and a 1989 claim, attributed to “Mike Guy” in an OEIS note, of ten million values (book not opened). None of these is progress on periodicity: finitely many instances of a universal claim move nothing, and the ‘sparse value’ observation is conditional. Flammenkamp's page itself says that if the sparse large values stop appearing, the sequence must become periodic. That is a conditional, not a result, and the page reports no pattern found in its log of G(n) ≥ 286. Neighbouring work does not reach this game. Dailly, Duchêne, Larsson and Paris (arXiv 2018, v3 2020) explicitly place Grundy's game outside their class, saying it is not in octal, because it needs unequal parts. Three 2026 subtraction-game and octal-game papers (Bhagat–Larsson–Manabe–Yamashita; Larsson–Manabe; Liang) do not mention Grundy's game on their abstract pages. For the AI search I ran 38 queries (listed below) covering the name, alternate names, result wording, and the places AI results are announced. No source names an AI system, lab or model in connection with this game. The closest lead was OpenAI's two 2026 releases. Its 1 August 2026 “Ten advances” (Astra) list has nine identified items, none on games; the tenth, per Zvi Mowshowitz's summary, is “Extremal number conjectures”, and the primary OpenAI page returned 403. Its 6 October 2026 openai/math repository (372 families) shows ten family titles in the fetched summary and a README with no games; the full family list (CONTENTS.md) was not readable, so a manuscript on this game cannot be excluded from what I read. Close calls: (a) whether the 2012 and 2026 computations move “a bound” — they extend the computed range, but per the scope rule a finite check of an all-n claim moves nothing; (b) whether the octal refresh moves the 235 figure — it moves it only relative to a 2009 figure, not in-window data; (c) the 1989 ten-million claim — its attribution is unverified and consistent with, not independent of, the 1996 run.
competing_reading: A reader could treat the computing record as substantial progress: the sequence has been computed to about 2.8×10¹¹ (the 2012 run), with sparse large values thinning out (1287 sparse values, the last at 48,399,022), and Flammenkamp states that if they die out the sequence must be periodic. On that reading the in-window table refresh and the OEIS tables to n = 200000 are evidence the question is close to resolved. The record does not support that reading: the sparse-value argument is conditional, the page does not show that the sparse values stop, and a finite computation of a universal claim moves nothing. A second reading would count the octal page's max n of 239 as a bound moved from Wikipedia's 235 (i.e. an in-window event). That moves a computed range that was already at 0–238 on the 2021 page, so the change is in the published figure, not in the mathematics.
what_would_settle_it: (1) A proof of eventual periodicity, with explicit N and p, or a proof of non-periodicity; either would answer the question directly. (2) A dated, readable statement from the 2025 Games of No Chance volume 71 entry for Grundy's game, which I could not read. (3) The text of Winning Ways pp. 96–97 and 111–112 and of Fair Game p. 96, to check the 1982 conjecture wording and the ten-million claim. (4) The openai/math CONTENTS.md family list, searched for “Grundy”, “Sprague”, “nim”. (5) A raw data comparison of Flammenkamp's 2021 and 2026 tables, to confirm no entry changed. (6) The OpenAI primary “ten advances” page, to close its tenth item. (7) Full texts of the 2026 papers by Liang and by Bhagat et al., to check for any mention of Grundy's game or of AI use.
